Get your answer and carry on, but Mr. Stamp is suggesting that you are slipping into the habit of leading on some important matters. If you could be careful about that in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since the minister appoints and relieves chiefs of SUP, when is there a situation in which you, on authority given to you by the minister, adopt decisions or pass decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I said in relation to this decision - I don't know what the transcript says - that on the 15th of April on the authority given to me by the minister I passed a decision to the effect that Cvetic would no longer be an employee. When the minister gave me such instructions or orders, then I would act accordingly; when he would tell me to make a decision in relation to a chief of a particular secretariat, that he should be dismissed, then acting upon instructions of the minister I would pass such decisions. So it's not just one decision. There are several decisions primarily relating to chiefs of secretariats in the territory of Kosovo, where after the minister's definite decision on the appointment of a new chief of secretariat, then I would pass a decision according to which the hitherto chief of secretariat would no longer be in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1036, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a decision dated the 20th of December, 1996, in which the chief of the department, Radovan Stojicic passes a decision whereby Ljubinko Cvetic, an employee of the Ministry of the Interior in Kragujevac, secretariat of the interior, is being sent to perform the tasks and duties of the chief of the Kosovska Mitrovica secretariat of the interior as of the 1st of January, 1997. It is important to note that the previous chief of department was deputy minister, whereas I was assistant minister. In the Serbian language and in our part of the world is a very important distinction. A deputy minister stands in for the minister, deputises for the minister, whereas the assistant minister assists the minister and is responsible for a particular activity. According to this decision, the deputy minister is practically minister when the minister is absent, and he has rights of his own and powers of his own in terms of making an appointment decision or a decision to relieve someone of duty, et cetera. That is a right that he has by virtue of the fact that he is deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a decision dated the 4th of June, 1997 whereby Minister Stojiljkovic is sending Bosko Petric to carry out the duties of the chief of the secretariat of the interior in Pristina as of the 15th of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have Exhibit P79, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a decision like the previous one for Cvetic. On the 15th of April, 1999, as authorised by the minister I make a decision to the effect that Colonel Bosko Petric shall no longer be chief of the secretariat of the interior in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have Exhibit P357.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is number 32 in your binder of documents. I would like us now to go through these rules, but you should explain to us how this worked out in practice and you should try to familiarise the Trial Chamber with this. We have before us the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. So could you please tell us what these rules regulate.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a rule book on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. It was adopted on the 31st of December, 1997. I have already said that in accordance with the authority vested in him by law, the minister of the interior, with the agreement of the Government of Serbia, passed these rules. These rules specifies the organisational units, their authority in terms of location, also their tasks and duties, and practically in this way these rules -- through these rules the minister prescribes how work will be organised and carried out in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether these rules pertain to both departments that are within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. These rules only pertain to the internal organisation of the public security. According to the regulations then in force, the internal organisation of the state security was organised on the basis of other rules which involve a certain degree of secrecy, so special rules are adopted, whereas these rules were passed for the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of the work carried out by public security, what is the basic organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the law, the basic organisational unit for carrying out work in the domain of public security is the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us about public security work. What organisational units were established for carrying out this work?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These rules specify two forms of organisational units, if I can put it that way. The first form is up and down the line, and the second form is territorial. As for the line-based one, it has to do with administrations in the headquarters of the ministry, and they are responsible for a particular line of work throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia; and then there is this other type of organisational units that are territorial organs of the Ministry of the Interior in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. Territorial organs are secretariats of the interior which then have their own organisational units deep down in the territories of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in the territory of the Republic of Serbia how many secretariats of the interior are there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These rules specify 33 secretariats in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, seven of which are in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, six in the territory of the autonomous province of Vojvodina, and the rest are in the territory of Serbia proper as it was known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And within the secretariat, are there other organisational units that cover parts of the territory within the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The secretariat of the interior was part of the ministry responsible for internal affairs in the territory of a few municipalities, that is to say immediately responsible for the headquarters of the secretariat and for a few municipalities. That is how the regional organisation worked at the time in the Republic of Serbia. So the secretariat of the interior had for its own region narrower organisational units that were in the territory of the municipalities that were an integral part of the said region. In the territory of the municipalities there were divisions of the interior. In larger municipalities, I think in about 20 in the territory of all of Serbia in smaller municipalities there were only police stations as an internal territorial form of organisation within the territory of the secretariat. So the secretariat and its narrower forms in bigger municipalities and in smaller municipalities with a smaller population, et cetera, there were only police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do these rules prescribe the actual authority of the secretariat or the division of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Secretariats and of course their divisions and police stations carried out all work from the domain of the interior in their own area. What was in the domain of work of the Ministry of the Interior according to law were also the tasks that were carried out by the secretariats of the interior and their narrower territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the organisational units within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior, the basic units were the administrations, just like there's the secretariat down there. In headquarters there were administrations. Every administration had a few divisions within it, so these were lower-ranking organisational units within the administrations. And every division had within it a few departments say for a particular group of tasks where this was required. So that was the schematic governing the organisation of the administrations in the headquarters of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, who headed the departments, the administrations, and the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They were headed by heads, the chief of the department, the head of the department; the chief of the administration, the head of the administration; the chief of the secretariat, the head of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the law says what all the administrations were so we don't have to go into that. From an operative point of view for the MUP and generally speaking for security, what are the most important administrations that were involved in operative security work?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since we've already been talking about the secretariats and we said that they carry out all the work in their own territory, from the domain of work of the interior, that is the protection of persons and property, the control of traffic, fire protection, checking the movement of foreigners, et cetera, so the secretariats did all of that within their own territory. For example, an administration would be involved only in one particular line of work. Say the crime police administration had as their duty to programme, promote the activity in this entire line of work, that is to say crime prevention throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia. The situation is that they would be responsible for crime prevention and control throughout the Republic of Serbia, and from that point of view it is their duty to promote such activities and issue certain instructions and orders to secretariats in terms of how this could be carried out as successfully as possible. That also pertains to the police administration and all the other administrations in the secretariat, or rather, at the headquarters of the ministry. In terms of the subject matter they deal with, the volume of their work, the complexity of their work, the first category of administrations in the headquarters of the ministry are the crime prevention police and the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to defence tasks, how did the Ministry of the Interior function and how was that implemented and regulated in practice?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, just like any other state organ in the Republic of Serbia, pursuant to the laws in force, was obligated to make preparations for an immediate peril of war and for war. And in that sense just like all other state organs they had their wartime plans. These wartime plans were technically prepared by an organisational unit within the Ministry of the Interior which was involved in defence preparations in the broader sense of that word. Before that used to be an independent unit and it was called a department for wartime preparations, but about the period that we are talking about now, which is 1997 and 1998, this job was done by a division within the police administration. So it was no longer an independent unit, but it rather operated within the police administration and their basic tasks were identical. This division had the duty to prepare programmes for the preparation of the Ministry of the Interior for operating in wartime conditions and in accordance with the regulations to prepare all the documents and to establish a system of conveying orders from the federal government all the way down to the state organs, as it was usually done in such circumstances. This division as far as the ministry is concerned, they prepared the plan at the headquarters which was always updated at a later stage by adding sometimes duties and tasks received from the federal government. These instructions had to be incorporated because all these plans were compatible with the system of preparing wartime plans that were carried out by the federal government to the level of republic to the level of the lowest organs. Now, that's as far as the headquarters is concerned. This organisational units had its sectors that were carrying out these jobs. As for the secretariat, this line of work was covered by officials within the police department that existed within any secretariat of the interior. So all the instructions and orders related to the preparation of wartime documents and their updating through this division in the police administration were passed down to the units on the ground, and therefore all the organs and the administrations within the headquarters had a duty to have the latest updated plans to make the Ministry of the Interior fully prepared in case of an immediate danger of war or war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This internal organisational structures within SUPs and OUPs, how did that look like and in what form did they operate?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The SUPs in order to be able to carry out their work successfully had at their headquarters in a way some kind of line-based divisions. So the difference is with the ministry [as interpreted] in Belgrade, between them and the ministry. The ministry [as interpreted] in Belgrade had the crime administration because they dealt with most of the problems, and the secretariat instead had divisions that dealt with this matter. So the internal organisational units in the secretariat for specific lines of work had divisions. For example, in the secretariat of the interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: One moment, please. On page 54, line 25, it should read not the ministry in Belgrade but the secretary in Belgrade and the same goes for line 24. So we are not talking about the ministry in Belgrade, we are talking about the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm waiting to have the witness concur with that, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's all right. I agree with this change. I was speaking about the secretariat of the interior and the criminal investigation police in the secretariat of the interior as a line-based organisation part dealing with the crime. At the level of the secretariat, apart from Belgrade there were divisions for combatting crime. Now, this line-based administration for combatting crime from the Ministry of the Interior through their line of work achieved betterment of the work through the respective divisions in the secretariat down there that were responsible for that operation. This is how this department and the headquarters of the ministry promoted and improved the work for which it was in charge with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started to explain the difference in the names of various organisational units in Belgrade and outside of Belgrade in various secretariats. Can you tell us why this distinction was made.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The distinction was made precisely because of the security problems that the secretariat faced. The most complex security issues in the Republic of Serbia had to be dealt by the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade and the crime combatting department. In order for these tasks to be successfully carried out by the secretariat in Belgrade, a large number of personnel was required and a large number of units and specialised skills were required. So the administration allowed within its organisational chart a large number of units and personnel in which way they would organise this line responsibility within the secretariat. All these jobs could have been done in the secretariat through the crime division within which we had economic crime sector, regular crime sector, et cetera. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please slow down. These are very complex matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, the complexity of what you were saying was going too quickly for the interpreters. Could you look back to the screen and take up where the interpretation fell away, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to speak slowly, first of all to allow the interpreters to hear you out and then to interpret what you are saying. If what you are saying is not interpreted and recorded, it's futile; therefore, I would kindly ask you just to repeat slowly your answer to my last question regarding the forms of internal organisational units and the distinction that existed between the Belgrade SUP and other SUPs throughout Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The most serious security-related issues in Serbia existed in the area of the secretariat of the interior [Real-time transcript read in error "failure to punish"] of Belgrade. In order for those tasks to be successfully completed, the organisational chart envisaged a large number of personnel and due to the complexity of these issues and the number of people involved in this work, the secretariat of the interior of Belgrade had administrations that were responsible for a certain type of work. Consequently, the secretariats that faced less serious security problems, these jobs in organisational terms were carried out by lower-ranking organisational units which in the secretariats were called divisions. These divisions within the secretariats encompassed practically all lines of work that existed in the Ministry of the Interior. Therefore, at the level of the secretariat --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we had a criminal investigation division --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel may consider whether or not line 3 of page 57 needs correction before we go too far away from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't want you to interrupt the witness who was attempting to describe a very complex situation. Yes, we see a failure to punish Belgrade may not be exactly what was meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before you continue, can you please - and my learned colleague is absolutely right - why there was an administration in Belgrade, whereas there was no such thing in the republic. Can you please slowly explain this segment.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 40 per cent of the security-related issues in the Republic of Serbia existed in the area of the secretariat in Belgrade. This involves the number of crimes committed, the misdemeanours, the traffic of offences in all lines of work. Such a complex security situation demanded a large number of personnel, and this large number of personnel and such problems that they faced could only have been organised by establishing administrations, because that's the highest level of organisation. And that was the case in Belgrade, the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade followed the same line. And they had the criminal investigating police administration, the police administration, the border police administration, fire-fighting police administration, which means that all those administrations that already existed in the ministry headquarters. Apart from the secretariat of the interior of Belgrade, we had other secretariats who for the performance of certain tasks along their lines of work had their respective organisational units that were called divisions. So there was in a secretariat a division of the criminal investigation police, whereas in Belgrade we had a criminal investigation administration. And also there was an administration at the level of the ministry. So in respective secretariats we had traffic division, criminal investigation division, et cetera, fire-fighting police division, border police division, the division for aliens and travel documents, et cetera. Sometimes if a secretariat didn't have so many problems of that nature instead of divisions, we had sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now explain the relationship between the administration at the ministry head office or headquarters and these divisions in the Belgrade SUP and other SUPs.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The ministry administration had the task and the responsibility for the security situation according to its line of work that stretched across the whole territory of the Republic of Serbia. In that way, it impacted on the preparation of plans for that particular line of work how to improve the operational performance of the secretariat along this specific line. They also received from various secretariats security-related information, and having analysed them they would send proposals to those secretariat for measures to be undertaken in order to monitor the security situation and launch proper response to such security problems. So this line within the ministry head office was responsible for the security situation according to its line of work all the way down to the last secretariat on the ground or let's say the last organisational unit within such a secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, were there any organisational units outside the headquarters of the secretariat; and if so, what were these organisational units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Outside the headquarters -- well, I don't really understand your question. Outside the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Outside the headquarters of the department.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were organisational units of the ministry. If I can put it this way, they were schools, namely, the post-secondary school for internal affairs, the police academy, the secondary school for internal affairs, and the security institute, and the department for legal and financial affairs. They were outside the public security department, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move on to a new topic now. I don't know whether you think it would be advisable to take the break now and then start this new topic, or should I start it now and then could we take the break later? I know that there's seven or eight minutes left until the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you are indicating that you're moving on to another fairly large area. That being the case, it would be more practical to have a break now and resume and allow you to go interrupted into the new area. That will give both you and the accused a chance to collect your thoughts again, separately of course. We will adjourn now and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, there is at 2.00 a ceremony in this courtroom to swear in a new Judge. For that reason, we are asked to finish early and somewhere about 1.30, 1.35, if that would fit in with your programme. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We now do have a topic that I believe will fit in to that time-frame more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I shall now like to move on to an article of the rules, which is Article 6, the Rules on Internal Organisation, that is a document 32 in your binder and it is P357, the exhibit number. What I would like you to tell us is how was this Article 6 applied in practice?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This article refers to the PJPs --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just to tell the Trial Chamber and the -- my learned colleagues it is page 7 in the English version. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So far we've been speaking about organisational units specified under these rules for the purpose of discharging their regular duties from Article 2 of these rules. In addition to these organisational units, according to Article 6 the minister was empowered and entitled to set up special "posebne" and special "specijalne" units of the police and other operative groups of the police. Pursuant to this article he adopted such documents as specified the tasks of the relevant units of the time-frames, the duties, the powers, and the rights and obligations of their personnel. If such units also comprised members of the reserve force, the possibility was also -- namely, the possibility was also provided for these units to be manned with members of the reserve force and as appropriate as necessary also by staff -- other staff from the -- within the Ministry of the Interior and the school of internal affairs. Thus, according to this article, the minister was authorised to set up special "posebne" and special "specijalne" police units and he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit P58 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is number 33.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Availing himself of the powers of this article of the rules, the minister of the interior, as can be seen on the following page, on the 1st of August 1993 - at that time it was Zoran Sokolovic - he brought a decision on the setting up of special units of the police. By this decision the place where these units will be set up is envisaged as well as the organisational and establishment structure of such units; the actual tasks of the special units are defined; who is entitled to put them in a state of alert, a state of readiness; who is the one who orders them to assemble and be engaged; how are they professionally trained, educated. The manner in which these units are manned is also specified in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 2 of this document defines the status of members of special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, were these -- or rather, what was the nature of these units that were set up by this decision?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The PJPs in the organs of the interior in the former Yugoslavia were set up after the incursion of an Ustasha terrorist group in 1972. At that time all the republican secretariats were charged with that task and set up units, special-purpose units, that could be used to discharge work, carry out tasks of the most complex security nature, which also included the apprehension and arrest of any terrorist groups. So in keeping with this obligation, the Ministry of the Interior in the time-period -- in that time-period always had units for this particular purpose under different names. These units were set up for those situations, for those complex security tasks which regular units were unable -- regular police units were unable to carry out. These units were intended for maintaining public law and order at mass rallies, football matches, large football matches. They were also envisaged to be used in the event of major natural disasters, in riots, mass riots and demonstrations. Also, it was envisaged that these units would be engaged to capture and deprive of liberty grave criminals, very serious criminals, and also in countering terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to ask you this: In terms of function and nature, were these standing units, permanent police structures?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These are units that were set up and structured according to a specific establishment scheme with companies, detachments, and platoons, and that was how they featured in the relevant report. It was always known whether someone was a member of that unit or not. In other words, these were not regular units, but they could be engaged depending on the security situation and assessment of that situation, meaning that they were engaged on an ad hoc basis. What does that mean? That means that if a problem crept up that could not be dealt with by using regular police units, the minister of the interior or a person so authorised by him under the law would order the engagement of a part of these already prepared and trained and equipped members of that unit to adequately react to the security problem at hand and deal with it. Once that problem has been resolved those units would return to their home secretariats and continue -- and resume their regular work and duties. So they are engaged and assemble as envisaged in the relevant documents only from the moment they start their engagement until they have completed the relevant security task.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us this: When they are not engaged, what work do these members of these units do?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These are regular -- they are regular staff of regular police stations, and their status is associated with a police station in which they charge their duties. They can be policemen who work as patrol, beat policemen; they can be engaged in traffic control or any other work which pertains to the uniformed police force. The minute they are in keeping with the relevant documents ascribed on the roster of members of special units, they undergo specific training in order to be able successfully to discharge the duties that I referred to earlier, starting with natural disasters, mass riots and disorders up -- and to terrorism. That means that during their work, in accordance with a plan of training, they are also educated and undergo training so that once orders are received for them to be engaged that they are capable successfully of discharging them. That is as far as the active part of the members of the special police force units are concerned. Every such unit, every police unit -- every such unit also has members of the reserve force among it who also undergo specific training, and they are engaged when so demanded -- when so ordered by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be so kind as to clarify two things for us: The first one is -- has to do with training of the PJP units. Who organises this training and how is it conducted?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the administration of the police at the headquarters of the ministry there exists an organisational form which is a department as a subunit or a section, the task of which is to see to the overall education of the PJPs and to ensure that they achieve the necessary level of readiness to successfully discharge complex tasks. The first task which is set before the future members of these units is the educational objective, their training in other words. The training and the programme of training are dealt with precisely in this organisation in the police administration. It draws up the curriculum, the training curriculum, which is then delivered at various secretariat areas on the territory of Serbia or in some special centres. And by completing that programme, the members of the PJPs, of the special police units, are practically trained for what expects -- for what awaits them in discharging their difficult duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst we are on the subject, the equipment and the armaments of these units, who sees to that? Whose concern is that? How is that dealt with?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is also the task of this particular organisational unit within the police administration of the Ministry of the Interior. There, depending on the purpose - and I described all the purposes a while ago - they're assigned adequate equipment. If their task is to re-establish law and order that has been disrupted, they will of course carry equipment which is adapted to that purpose. The particular type of equipment that the PJPs will have, depending on their specific task that they should be assigned to, all these and all this was programmed and planned by this particular unit within the police administration, and it also monitors the purchase, the procurement, of the different types of equipment that was to be obtained, and saw to the uniformity of both the equipment and the armaments of the PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please explain to us in practice, what was the engagement of the PJPs like on a concrete task? But please explain it to us without reference to specifically Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: One of the basic tasks on which the PJPs were engaged is in fact maintaining law and order at large rallies or action in -- when demonstrations or protests were taking place or situations where law and order was disrupted and ended in demonstrations. An assessment would be made in the ministry of the future security event, for instance, some demonstrations in Belgrade. In accordance with the assessments that he receives, the minister -- that is assessments regarding the possible number of people that will turn out at the demonstrations -- the minister would be given an assessment of the required number of people to adequately respond to that number of protesters. Then the minister issues instructions or an order as to what units and in what number will be engaged to maintain law and order at such demonstrations or in order to suppress such demonstrations. In accordance with that order, members of the special police units, two or three or what have you, number of detachments, then arrive in Belgrade. There they are provided accommodation. The secretariat in Belgrade has its headquarters, its staff set up specifically to act in respect to that particular security-related issue and has its relevant plan. These units, when they come in the area of Belgrade, are resubordinated to that particular staff and they act in accordance with the tasks issued them in accordance with a plan adopted by that staff. Until that security matter has been dealt with, these units remain in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When they come to discharge a task, to whom do these units answer, and who is in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the secretariat in Belgrade had a staff that was in charge of acting in relation to that security-related incident. All would be tasked with reporting to that staff, and they are placed at the disposal of that staff. Practically, in an operative sense, from then onwards as for their engagement and all decisions related to it, all decisions are made by this staff that is in charge in terms of territory of acting with regard to such security-related incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When units are sent to carry out a particular task, do they have any functional link with the organisational units, say the SUPs or the OUPs from which they were sent to carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when they are engaged, their obligations stop, their obligations of the members of the PJPs, towards the secretariat from which they were sent. So they have only obligations towards the secretariat or staff to which they have been sent by way of assistance. They have no obligations whatsoever anymore towards their own organisational units or the secretariat from which they had been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When these units accomplish the mission they had been sent out on, do they send reports to the secretariats from which they had been sent?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. All the reports that they are supposed to submit in relation to that particular security-related incident, they submit to the staff that is in charge of dealing with that security-related incident. The commanders of these units can perhaps send a report to their original secretariat if there were some disciplinary problems or, I don't know, some kind of secondary behaviour of the members involved. However, in terms of operative procedure their only obligation is towards the staff where they had been engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the decision on the engagement of PJP units is passed by the minister or a person authorised to do so by the minister. After such a decision, what is the technology that follows in terms of procedure, in terms of carrying out that decision?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a legal term as to who can engage these units and that's the way it's always been. Without the minister's decision, not a single part of the PJPs can be used in any way. I'm sorry, the other part of your question slipped my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After that what was the technology, as it were, of the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Once a decision is made by the minister, the organisational unit within the police administration that I spoke of a few moments ago and that took care of training and equipment, carries out all the necessary work, that is, calling up members of the unit so that they could respond in accordance with the minister's decision. They should report to a particular secretariat, a particular area where they're to be engaged. This task consists of the following: This organisational unit should send orders to the secretariats to mobilise a company, a platoon, or, I don't know, whatever. They give instructions by way of a dispatch as to how that unit should be equipped, that is to say the members who are being sent. Also, what means of transportation would be used, and also their possible rights in terms of per diems and the like. It has to do with logistics primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that there is a plan, a plan of action. Who approves that plan of action and on what basis?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If we take the example of Belgrade and establishing peace and order in Belgrade, such a plan is approved of the chief of secretariat in Belgrade and its operationalisation is carried out by the staff there. Of course if there is a special security situation on the ground, then the minister should also be made aware of the plan, that is to say he should state his own views in this regard as well, but basically it is the chief of the secretariat involved that is responsible for carrying out the said task in his own area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this plan is adopted, does -- is a decision made on the engagement of the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the proper sequence of events. In order to make a plan, first there has to be an estimate of the number of people who might get together for a rally or a riot or whatever, and in relation to that a security response is planned. Based on such an estimate of the necessary security forces, a request is put to the minister as to how many people should be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing, when the administration of the ministry that is in charge of such tasks, when they do everything that you told us about, where they're sent and how they're sent, does it have any powers in relation to the PJP unit sent on that particular mission?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That part of the administration of the police that deals with bringing in members of the PJP to the secretariat where the operation is going to take place has the duty towards the staff of that ministry to tell them when the forces would arrive, at what time, what the numbers of personnel would be, et cetera. Then the role of that organisational units in the police administration boils down to the following: To engage people, to make it possible for them to get to the secretariat from which they would operate, and that this staff should be told, "At such and such a time members of the police will come to you," et cetera. Also the role of the organisational unit involved is a logistical one. If additional forces are needed or if additional equipment is needed, they are going to help out operationally. So if this staff is, say, in Belgrade, they are going to help them carry out this duty as successfully as possible. But operationally, it is that staff that is responsible for carrying out this task, or rather, this secretariat in whose territory the activity is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After the task is carried out, the PJP unit that was engaged, does it submit a report to the police administration about its engagement, about its activity?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Operationally, no. That is to say, everything that was done by this unit operationally, it is done in relation to that staff so that this staff could compile a complete report. The leadership of that PJP will submit a report if some of the equipment was damaged or again if there is an obligation to renew something. That is what I meant. But operationally, how they operated, in which way they carried out these tasks, this attached unit of the PJP has such obligations towards the staff where they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a brief question because our time is running out. You said that the police administration addressed the SUPs from which the units were engaged in order to be sent to carry out a particular task. Did the SUPs inform the police administration to the effect that they had carried out this order and that they mobilised the units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because in the secretariat there is a group of people -- at least there is one person who takes care of the special units in his own area in this sense, where they were sent, whether they were equipped properly, where these reports are, et cetera. And then there is this mutual information. There is an exchange of information between the police administration that is involved in this work and these employees in the territory of the secretariat from which these members of the unit were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to call it a day now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic, yes. We will adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
